Chin and jaw
A strike to the point of the chin or the side of the jaw turns the head sharply. The brain lags behind the skull, which is what causes a knockout. The jaw is the target of most finishing punches.
Hook or cross to the side of the jaw; uppercut under the chin when the head comes forward.
Temple
The side of the head above the ear, where the skull is thinnest. Kicks and hooks that land here are very dangerous, which is why the guard covers it with the gloves.
High roundhouse or question mark kick over the guard; hooks around it; spinning backfist.
Solar plexus
The soft spot under the breastbone, above the stomach. A straight shot here pushes into the diaphragm and knocks the wind out: the opponent cannot breathe for a few seconds.
Straight shots: the cross to the body, the teep, the spinning back kick, a straight knee in the clinch.
Liver

Under the lowest ribs on the opponent's right side, in front of your lead hand (orthodox against orthodox). A clean shot causes a delayed, overwhelming pain that drops fighters while they are still conscious.
Lead hook to the body, lead (switch) body kick, a straight knee; dip your level to reach it.
Ribs and spleen
The opponent's left side, open to your rear kick and rear hand. The floating ribs at the bottom are not joined to the breastbone and break or bruise easily; the spleen sits behind them.
Rear roundhouse kick to the body, rear hook or uppercut to the body.
Thigh (lead leg)
The big muscle on the outside of the lead thigh. Repeated low kicks there deaden the leg: the opponent cannot push off it, so their punches and movement lose power.
Rear low roundhouse with the shin, a few centimetres above the knee; set it up with punches to the head.
Calf (lead leg)
The back and outside of the lead calf, just below the knee. It is hard to check because it lands below the knee, and a few clean kicks take away the opponent's stance and footwork.
The calf kick: a short low roundhouse when their weight is on the lead leg.
